short: The first two and a half centuries of empire, ruled by a man who insisted he was only the first citizen.
full:
Augustus never called himself emperor. The settlement he built after Actium left the Senate, the consulships and the old republican offices standing, and took for himself a bundle of powers — command of the frontier provinces, the authority of a tribune, the title princeps, first citizen — that added up to sole rule while denying that anything had changed. The fiction mattered: it gave the regime a language in which Romans could accept it.

The arrangement held for a remarkably long time. Under it Rome absorbed Britain, annexed Dacia, reached its greatest extent under Trajan, and spent the second century in something close to peace. It also never solved succession. There was no rule for choosing a princeps, so each transfer of power was improvised — by adoption when it went well, by the army when it did not.

The Principate ends where that improvisation finally failed. In 235 the murder of Severus Alexander by his own troops opened fifty years in which the throne belonged to whoever the legions were currently paying.
